title: Isotopes, Isobars, Isotones and Isodiaphers
topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: The family of 'same/different' atom pairs that the nuclear model makes possible — definitions, examples and exam traps. These follow directly from the concepts of Z and A.
• **Isotopes** (same Z, different A): ¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl; ¹²C/¹³C/¹⁴C; ²³⁵U/²³⁸U. Same chemical properties (same electronic configuration), different physical properties and different mass.
• **Isobars** (same A, different Z): ⁴⁰Ar (18 p) and ⁴⁰Ca (20 p); ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N. Different elements, same mass number — different chemical properties.
• **Isotones** (same neutron number N = A − Z): ³⁶S, ³⁷Cl, ³⁸Ar, ³⁹K, ⁴⁰Ca (all N = 20); ³H and ⁴Li (N = 2).
• **Isodiaphers** (same difference N − Z): ²³⁹U and ²³⁵Th (N − Z = 51); ²³⁵U and ²³¹Th.
• (Bonus) **Isoelectronic species** (same electron count): N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ — all 10 electrons.

Rutherford's nucleus separates identity (Z) from mass (A = Z + N). Once the neutron was found (1932), atoms of one element could differ in mass (isotopes) and atoms of different elements could share a mass number (isobars) — resolving the contradictions that Dalton's 'identical atoms' postulate created.

Isotopes are chemically almost identical (the electrons decide chemistry) but differ in nuclear stability (¹⁴C decays, ¹²C does not) — the basis of carbon dating, radioisotope tracers (¹³¹I in thyroid studies, ⁶⁰Co in radiotherapy) and isotope separation by mass (gaseous diffusion of UF₆). Isobars, being different elements, are chemically completely different.

Average mass = Σ(fractional abundance × isotopic mass). Chlorine: 0.75 × 35 + 0.25 × 37 = 35.5 u; neon: 0.905 × 20 + 0.0027 × 21 + 0.0923 × 22 ≈ 20.18 u. The fractional pattern explains why most atomic masses are not whole numbers — Dalton's 'identical atoms in whole-number ratios' fails here.
confusion: ❌ Isotopes have different chemical properties. ✅ Nearly identical chemically; they differ in mass and nuclear stability.
❌ Isobars are atoms of the same element. ✅ Same A but different Z — different elements entirely.
❌ Isotones are defined by equal protons. ✅ Equal neutron number (N = A − Z).
❌ ¹²C and ¹⁴C belong to different elements. ✅ Both are carbon (Z = 6); ¹⁴C is simply radioactive.

universalFacts: Carbon dating uses the ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio (half-life 5730 years).
³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl in a 3 : 1 ratio gives the familiar 35.5 u average mass.
Radio-iodine ¹³¹I concentrates in the thyroid because it is chemically indistinguishable from ordinary iodine.
examples: **Problem:** Boron is 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B. Find its atomic mass. **Solution:** 0.20 × 10 + 0.80 × 11 = 10.8 u — matching the tabulated 10.81 u.
**Problem:** Show that ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N are isobars. **Solution:** ¹⁴C: Z = 6, N = 8, A = 14; ¹⁴N: Z = 7, N = 7, A = 14 — same A, different Z.
importantNotes: State the defining quantity first (Z, A, N, N − Z) — the four names are easy to mix up.
Connect isotopes back to Dalton's limitation: identical atoms of an element is the false postulate.

summary: Once the nucleus separates identity (Z) from mass (A = Z + N), four families of related atoms become definable. Isotopes share Z and differ in A (¹H/²H/³H, ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl, ¹²C/¹³C/¹⁴C, ²³⁵U/²³⁸U) and are chemically almost identical, since electrons govern chemistry, but differ in mass and nuclear stability — the basis of ¹⁴C dating, ¹³¹I thyroid therapy and ⁶⁰Co radiotherapy. Isobars share A and differ in Z (⁴⁰Ar with ⁴⁰Ca, ¹⁴C with ¹⁴N), so they are entirely different elements chemically. Isotones share the neutron number N = A − Z (³⁶S, ³⁷Cl, ³⁸Ar, ³⁹K, ⁴⁰Ca all have N = 20). Isodiaphers share the difference N − Z (²³⁹U and ²³⁵Th, both N − Z = 51). A bonus family is isoelectronic species with equal electron counts, such as N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺, all with 10 electrons.
importantConcepts: Isotopes: same Z, different A — same element, nearly identical chemistry, different mass and stability
Isobars: same A, different Z — different elements entirely, e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca, ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N
Isotones: same neutron number N = A − Z, e.g. ³⁶S, ³⁷Cl, ³⁸Ar, ³⁹K and ⁴⁰Ca, all with N = 20
Isodiaphers: same difference N − Z, e.g. ²³⁹U and ²³⁵Th, both with N − Z = 51
Isoelectronic species: same electron count, e.g. N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ with 10 electrons each
importantStatements: The defining quantity must be stated first: Z for isotopes, A for isobars, N for isotones, N − Z for isodiaphers.
Isotopes are chemically almost identical but differ in mass and in nuclear stability.
Isobars are different elements, so their chemical properties are completely different.
Isotopes contradict Dalton's postulate that all atoms of an element are identical in mass.
Average atomic mass = Σ(fractional abundance × isotopic mass), which is why most atomic masses are not whole numbers.

keyPoints: Write the four definitions as 'same Z / same A / same N / same N − Z' and the four names follow.
Chlorine's 3 : 1 isotopic ratio produces the familiar 35.5 u average mass.
¹⁴C/¹²C dating uses a half-life of 5730 years; ¹³¹I concentrates in the thyroid because it is chemically ordinary iodine.
Uranium enrichment by gaseous diffusion of UF₆ separates ²³⁵U from ²³⁸U purely by mass.
specialNotes: Isotones must be computed as A − Z for each nuclide; ³⁶S has Z = 16, so N = 20, matching ⁴⁰Ca with Z = 20.
¹²C and ¹⁴C are isotopes of one element, not of different elements — both have Z = 6.
Isodiaphers are the rarest of the four terms and are usually only asked as a one-mark definition.
examShortTricks: Tabulate the four families with 'same quantity, different quantity' — this matches the marking scheme.
To test a pair, compute Z, A and N = A − Z for each and compare.
Mention Dalton's postulate by name whenever isotopes are discussed.
